did_you_know.text: The word shever here is not related to breaking; it refers to buying grain and food. This is an ancient use of the Hebrew root sh-b-r.
Judah accepts personal responsibility for Benjamin. The phrase “you may demand him from my hand” presents complete accountability, as though Benjamin were entrusted to him.
“The choice produce of the land” means its finest products. Gifts like these were also a way to show respect and ease relations between important people.
The gifts include balm, honey, aromatic resins, pistachios, and almonds. Some of these names refer to resins or spices and do not necessarily mean exactly the products we call by those names today.
The brothers take both the money returned to their sacks and additional money. In this way they try to show that they are honest and prevent another mistake in the transaction.
Joseph orders a meal to be prepared at noon, when many people in the ancient Near East ate their main meal of the day. Inviting guests to a feast was an important sign of honor.
The word matmon means a treasure or something valuable kept in storage. Joseph’s steward calms the brothers by describing the returned money as a blessing from their father’s God.
Washing guests’ feet and providing fodder for their donkeys were customary acts of hospitality in the ancient world. After travel on dusty roads, this was both practical and respectful.

The phrase “his compassion was stirred” describes a powerful emotional reaction. In biblical Hebrew, compassion is sometimes connected with the womb, so the feeling is pictured as rising from within the body.

The meal is divided into three groups: Joseph, his brothers, and the Egyptians. The text calls eating with Hebrews an “abomination” to the Egyptians, but it does not specify exactly what caused this cultural taboo.
Benjamin receives a portion five times larger than those of his brothers. This unusual serving highlights his favored position at the meal and prepares the way for the test in the next chapter.
